A cutting-edge, super-low emittance beamline is being developed for the CSNS synchrotron at Shanghai, featuring an innovative TM110 cavity that utilizes deflecting mode cavitation to manipulate the particle beam's phase space, thereby enhancing focusing capabilities. The goal is to attain an even dispersion in the horizontal plane, ultimately enabling researchers to precisely analyze and correct the beam's dynamics using sophisticated inversion techniques. For this purpose, detailed computational models have been created to analyze the performance of the new cavity unit, focusing on both resonator properties and their influence on beam dynamics. The study's findings on the new cavity unit will be extensively discussed, including comparisons with traditional quadrupole units.

Predicting pedestrian trajectories based on observations has several significant applications in multiple domains. Most current studies focus on developing sophisticated models for trajectory estimation but often overlook data quality and the limitations of training datasets. Top-performing models can produce a wide range of implausible trajectories due to their high capacity and lack of constraints in training data. We address this shortcoming by introducing a trajectory filtering framework that can be applied to any existing trajectory estimation model to produce more accurate predictions. This approach utilizes a separate self-supervised trajectory learning model to identify realistic trajectories and eliminate unrealistic ones, thereby improving overall performance in trajectory estimation. We evaluated the proposed framework on multiple datasets and found a notable enhancement in performance. We also compared the proposed method to other existing techniques and provided a thorough analysis of different training configurations to support our conclusions with extensive ablation studies.

A key aspect of statistical mechanics lies in the concept of complexity, which can be used to measure the degree of pattern information contained within a system. Various methods for calculating complexity on a Boltzmann machine have been developed, which involves a type of neural network. This paper investigates the complexity of a Boltzmann machine using a novel metric called the average pattern error. By introducing a dynamic Boltzmann machine with adjustable parameters, the paper demonstrates complexity on this model and derives mathematical equations to describe its relationship to the parameters. The results show that the complexity of the dynamic system can be affected in different ways by various parameters and dynamics. The paper also discusses how the choice of learning algorithm may impact the final complexity of the system.

Our approach adjusts the spacing between robots participating in a swarm operation that necessitates proximity to obstacles, without restricting their movement within the defined boundary. By incorporating a rule for maintaining a standardized distance among the robots, the density of the swarm is optimized, yielding a more uniform distribution and better proximity to obstacles, which in turn enables more efficient navigation. This adjustment also enables the swarm to effectively traverse narrower areas and retain its structure even through changes in density. When applied to swarms of robots interacting with physical environments, the benefit is a more efficient and productive operation within the defined boundary. A model simulating various scenarios, as well as a real-world experiment using a robot capable of mapping its environment, have been employed to validate the advantage of adjusting the spacing among the robots.

Automated healthcare analysis can significantly reduce the risk of misdiagnosis and
accelerate medical diagnosis and treatment. The analysis of blood tests is a vital area
that necessitates precise pattern recognition and measurement. We utilize a cutting-edge
deep learning approach to develop a comprehensive system for blood test analysis.
By combining the capabilities of fully convolutional networks and sliding-window
techniques, we create a system that can accurately identify blood regions and capture
important details. We also employ a novel, multi-scale deep learning framework called
DlCellNet to analyze the composition of blood cells. DlCellNet utilizes a generalized
multiple instance learning model to leverage the patterns within aggregates of blood
cell images. Through a thorough evaluation using 15 different metrics on two distinct
datasets, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods
in both visual coarsening metrics and cell classification tasks. Furthermore, our
technique produces satisfactory results on novel, unseen datasets.

A variational approximation is made for the adiabatic gauge potential, with parametric dependence determined through minimization of nested commutators' squared Frobenius norms, and it is demonstrated that this potential varies smoothly with the adiabatic parameter. Utilizing the approximated gauge potential, a hierarchy of anisotropic Berry-Esseen theorems is developed and applied to the Blum-Shrivastava model to yield an upper bound on the Kolmogorov distance between the eigenstate measure and its non-linear approximation, resulting in rates of convergence of $N^{-1}$, $N^{-3/2}$, and $N^{-5/2}$ for orders 0, 1, and 2, respectively. Furthermore, an anisotropic limit theorem is established for smooth observables, and it is shown that limits can be taken in both the adiabatic and asymptotic directions independently of one another.

A phenomenon called chromatic aberration, found in human eyes and some image filters, causes a separation of colors into different focal points, which has also been observed in pinhole cameras. This effect divides an image into multiple planes, each displaying a different color. This research aims to understand the psychological and visual effects of this phenomenon by presenting a method to simulate it in images. A demonstration of this method can be found at the link https://github.com/kevincalabria/chromatic-aberation. The resulting simulation reveals that this effect makes warm colors appear more distant and cool colors appear more close, which can be explained by a connection to the traditional association of red with warmth and blue with coldness. Furthermore, this method allows for the creation of engaging visual effects that can enhance image rendering, particularly in images or videos of fire, water, or electromagnetic phenomena, which can also enable new applications in image processing.

This article presents a new approach to proving the convergence of several infinite series and sums that involve the Ramanujan beta and gamma functions, as well as the $C^{\lambda}$ functions, under specific conditions. Furthermore, this method can be employed to establish some upper bounds for these series and sums. Using the obtained results, two series expansions are derived for the $C^{\lambda}$ functions, as well as the $C$ function, which involve coefficients of two different types. Additionally, the infinite single sums are calculated that yield the basic hypergeometric functions $\(_2F_1$ and $\tilde{_2F_1}$, and the $C$ function, under certain conditions. Moreover, the $C^{\lambda}$ functions are expressed using the given sums, infinite series, areas, and a few other special functions, including the Appell's hypergeometric functions and the Mathieu's C and E series, through the Lambert W function.

A closed surface $M$ with a metric in three dimensions and non-negative curvature is considered. It is demonstrated that if the surface's curvature is positive or the topological structure is that of the two-sphere, then it can be conformally transformed into the three-sphere. Conversely, if this conformal transformation exists, then either the original surface has positive curvature or it is topologically equivalent to the two-sphere. A result for surfaces of bounded upper curvature is also obtained, showing that it is conformally equivalent to the two-sphere under specific curvature conditions.

Researchers have proposed a novel concept for a hard X-ray undulator, enabled by the output of a short-pulse laser-wakefield accelerator that produces a high-energy electron beam. The electron beam, delivered from the accelerator, serves as the radiation source for the undulator, yielding an extremely short, high-energy, and high-brightness photon beam. This allows the development of ultrafast, high-energy hard X-ray free-electron lasers, potentially eclipsing the current state-of-the-art in this field. The unique characteristics of the laser-generated electron beam also facilitate the creation of a high-energy, sub-10-femtosecond seed pulse for a next-generation high-power laser plasma particle accelerator, addressing a critical challenge associated with such a challenging technology.

In our two-part series on the $h\to\gamma\gamma$ phenomenon, we initially demonstrated how observations from this phenomenon at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) impose significant constraints on dark sectors with broken $Z_2$ symmetry, with the second part exploring theoretical implications in detail. This is particularly true for the lightest Majorana fermion $\chi$ as the primary source of bi-linear neutrino Yukawa coupling which ultimately influences Higgs coupling strength with Standard Model leptons. By establishing a relationship between this Higgs coupling $h$ and photons, and the breaking of $Z_2$ symmetry, we find that the Higgs coupling approaches its Standard Model limits only when the $Z_2$ symmetry breaking is sufficiently large. Furthermore, our analysis using LHC constraints has shown that the $Z_2$ symmetry breaking must be sufficiently large, with the $h\to\gamma\gamma$ phenomenon playing a crucial role here. This is particularly true for Majorana mass doublets where the dark sector responsible for the $h$ Higgs boson interacts with Standard Model leptons only through the bi-linear or goebel-type Yukawa coupling. As a result of this, we find that the $h$ Higgs boson tends to decay to photons preferentially over $h\to b\bar{b}$ in cases where the dark sector is Majoronic with the goebel-type Yukawa coupling, with the $h$ Higgs

We build on the foundation of universal data exchange solutions, which guarantee consistency and existence, by introducing a novel concept - key covered. A key covered property ensures that a specific data aspect is present in every target schema. The introduction of key covered keys adds flexibility to the data exchange approach, allowing it to accommodate various desirable outcomes. The key covered property has a significant impact on the data exchange solutions, as it affects their consistency and existence when applied to certain source and target schemas. Specifically, adding key covered properties can ensure consistency and an guaranteed maximum number of solutions. Interestingly, key covered properties also reveal cases where the traditional data exchange solutions fail to exist or become infinite.

This discussion presents a newly developed Python package, pyStoNED, designed to facilitate seamless integration of various regression techniques offered by SciPy. pyStoNED effectively minimizes complexity by simplifying the transfer of data from one format to another, allowing users to easily perform multivariate regression analyses with minimal intervention. Additionally, we highlight our approach to nonlinear multivariate regression using a linear-contrast regularization method, which utilizes a nonlinear model with a linear approximation. This approximation-based approximation technique effectively transforms the problem into a solvable linear regression framework. To validate our method, we applied the proposed technique to separate the absorption and scattering components of cultures containing light-emitting microorganisms. This resulted in the successful calculation of intrinsic specific growth rates and fluorescence signals.

Predictive models that include non-abelian extensions of the Standard Model can successfully explain the origin of neutrino mass and baryon asymmetry. This discussion will focus on the scalar sector of one such model, where non-abelian gauge groups $SU(N_V) \wedge SU(N_L)$ generate Yukawa interactions with fermions and scalars. The scalar sector consists of three light self-conjugate fields and one heavy singlet. The light scalars have small CP-even and CP-odd Yukawa couplings to neutrinos, while the heavy scalar has substantial CP-conserving couplings to Standard Model particles. This discussion will demonstrate that future High Luminosity LHC data can set stringent limits on the light scalars' interactions, specifically, it will show that the scalar's Yukawa coupling to neutrinos will either be greatly constrained or will fall within a narrow range by 2025. During this time period, exclusion limits for CP-even and CP-odd Yukawa couplings will be comparable, however it is anticipated that the CP-odd coupling will eventually surpass the CP-even coupling due to increased sensitivity from neutrinoless double beta decay and reactor neutrino experiments. Following its completion in the late 2030s, ILC will have the capability to precisely measure the ratio of Yukawa couplings between the light and heavy scalars, providing a substantial advancement in our understanding of the scalar sector.

Recently, outside-in parsing has gained popularity for analyzing image meanings. Outside-in parsing typically employs pre-trained object detectors and linguistic models to propose parse trees based on tree structures. A cutting-edge outside-in parsing method, FPIO, utilizes a few-shot learning technique and has shown exceptional performance. When trained with a small number of annotated trees, FPIO outperforms other existing few-shot parsing methods, showcasing robust performance even when the number of annotated trees reaches 32. Furthermore, FPIO delivers superior results to state-of-the-art object detectors and outside-in parsing methods trained with a large number of annotated images. Analysis reveals that FPIO's unique transfer knowledge has a positive impact on parsing performance.

This study investigates how diverse data impacts the resilience of speech recognition models. We find that using data from multiple sources with varying speaker accents, dialects, and topics enables these models to perform well across different domains, even as the vocabulary and spoken topics continue to shift over time. Consequently, using a diverse data set can help reduce the need for frequent model updates in dynamic environments. Building on this insight, we designed an unsupervised method to guide the data selection process, which prioritizes data samples that minimize the model's differences before and after training on the new data. In internal tests, this data selection strategy surpassed random selection and training on extended versions of the standard Switchboard corpus. Finally, we explored data selection as a regularisation technique and observed that training on a subset of the data can be more effective than training on the entire dataset, especially when the model remains accurate after training on new data with changed topics.

Using radial velocity curves, researchers discovered the binary systems 19\,V Camelopardalis and HD\,205422, and identified them as members of a specific category of stars. Based on observations with modern instruments, their characteristics are as follows. 19\,V Camelopardalis, classified as a Be-type star, has an orbital period of 211.58 days and frequency of $4.713 \pm 0.005 \times 10^{-8}\mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. In contrast, HD\,205422, resembling a normal Be star, has an orbital period of 42.86 days and frequency of $7.654 \pm 0.007 \times 10^{-8}\mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Notably, the orbital periods of these binary systems fall within a specific range, indicating the existence of a different type of stellar arrangement. Furthermore, by employing SEVMAP and FEVMAP, a novel technique for analyzing frequency patterns via murmur detection has been developed using graph theory and unsupervised machine learning. Murmur frequencies were discovered in the spectra of these binary systems, and their characteristics were defined mathematically. Murmurs may appear as regular variations in radial velocity curves and could potentially be detected in observed data. In the case of 19\,V Camelopardalis, FEVMAP identified 14 low-amplitude frequency patterns, and in HD\,205422, FEVM

Although out-of-domain data augmentation techniques can enhance the performance of Internet-Tuning models, they still rely on in-domain data for pretraining and may struggle with new samples. To overcome this limitation, this paper presents an online data augmentation technique that uses in-domain generative models to create high-quality augmented samples. We implement this method within Internet-Tuning adapters and observe significant improvements in out-of-domain zero-shot and few-shot classification tasks, now matching the performance of ideal, fully-tuned models. Furthermore, the approach's efficiency enables applications in online and streaming scenarios where resources are limited. We also detail the implementation of a web service that uses this technique to enhance model performance through continuous data augmentation. We publicly share our code and data augmentation web service at https://github.com/jacobkiefer/data-augmentation-webservice.

The purpose of this research paper is to establish a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator in the context of the first moment. Specifically, this inequality can be expressed as $\lambda_{1,\mu}^{(1)}\left(\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\right) \le c_N \sum_{i=1^N} \lambda_{i,\mu}(x_i)^{d+2} $ where the parameters $N, d \in \mathbb{N}$ define a multivariable Hermite operator with parameters $\mu$. Here, $\lambda_{i,\mu}$ denotes the $i$th eigenvalue of the given operator with corresponding eigenfunction $\varphi_{i,\mu}$. Constants $c_N$ are solved for in the given scenario and general cases. Furthermore, this analysis leads to the determination of conditions under which the known geometric configurations that yield the minimum first eigenvalue are also optimal in this alternative context.

Neural tangent kernels (NTKs) offer a method to approximate complex deep neural networks with more predictable properties, like continuous gradients and reproducible behavior. This approximation enables theoretical generalizations of NTKs, leading to more interpretable models that can tackle larger datasets and diverse distributions with improved robustness. In this study, we apply these theoretical advancements to a variety of machine learning scenarios, effectively converting challenging problems into solvable, closed-form expressions with improved interpretability. Initially, we apply our generalization of NTKs to regression problems and demonstrate superior performance on regression tasks as well as text classification when compared to standard NTKs. Next, we convert classification NTKs to kernelized versions, specifically enabling us to analyze their bias-variance characteristics and make informed parameterization decisions with associated optimization complexity analyses. This yields significant improvements in state-of-the-art performance for binary and multi-class classifications, and we observe an inherent correlation between log-loss and bias-variance, leading to a promising prospect for general, model-agnostic calibration in deep neural networks.

The extended Hatano-Nelson chain, consisting of units with complex unbalanced hopping, leads to unique behaviors in both its local and non-local responses. By analyzing the response to a time-dependent electric field, it is found that site-specific correlations induce an varied distribution of current within the chain. This, in turn, causes the current to be influenced by the distance to the terminus of individual sites, resulting in an varying effective resistance as sites near the terminus experience a "skin effect." Furthermore, an additional random potential is applied to the sites, giving rise to non-Hermitian chiral quantum matter with "fractonic" behavior, characterized by a rigid percolating structure. This condition is reflected in the absence of long-range interactions within the site-less Green's function. By using Green's function theory, it is found that site-less correlations can result in an observed "skin effect" and can cause a partial screening of the random potential within the site-less framework, resulting in an effective site-less Hamiltonian. By applying the Fock-diagonalization method, it is found that the site-less Hamiltonian can be mapped to a one-dimensional interacting fermion model with a "skin effect," displaying unique energy gap and renormalization properties.

Our investigation focuses on exploring a synthesized speech listener's strategy
in pinpointing a woman's level of professionalism through tone perception. By use
of a crowdsourced task on Amazon's MTurk platform, we've identified specific vocal
traits - articulation, rate, energy, and pitch - that contribute to competence perception
in a female speech model.  To simulate variations in these vocal traits, we've made
use of a vector arithmetic approach that enables the blending of pre-existing vocal
characteristics to create novel combinations.  Results from a subsequent perception
study indicate that blending distinct vocal features has a substantial impact on the
perception of professionalism, revealing significant correlations between the level
of blending and perceived competence.  Our findings also suggest that the intensity
of the voice, when modified by other characteristics, has the greatest influence on the
perception of someone being professional.

We present a model of a heavy iso-singlet Higgs boson to address the anomalies seen in the distribution of inner galactic dark matter events as observed by the DIRECTORAT NATIONAL DE LA RECHERCHE SUR L'ENERGIE DE LA FUSION (DIRAC) experiment. The proposed model utilizes a heavy dark matter particle, specifically an ultralight axion-like particle, to achieve stability. In this work, we analyze how the model's characteristics affect its potential for detection in high-energy collisions at the LARGE Hadron Collider and future facilities, as well as possible constraints from astronomical observations, focusing specifically on the galactic dark matter event anomalies and dark matter direct detection experiments.

This research explores how introducing a fundamental minimum for length impacts the energy level patterns observed in nuclear spinning, drawing on $SU(1,1)$ bosonic theory. To investigate this interaction, we utilize two methods: analyzing how the ground state of the harmonic oscillator changes as the minimum length varies, and applying $\mathcal{L}_p^s$ for a specific nuclear model, the Nilsson model. In both approaches, we examine the impact of the minimum length on energy levels, observing that these levels either decrease or remain constant as the angular momentum increases, provided that the minimum length does not exceed a certain threshold. This investigation also identifies a limiting point beyond which further increases in the angular momentum cannot occur. In addition, we compared the energy spectra generated by the bosonic theory to those predicted by triaxial nuclei, revealing some similarities in energy behavior but also some distinct differences in structural patterns. To establish a universal relationship between energy levels and the angular momentum, we developed a linear approximation for energy spectra.

Research into multivariate Golay complementary array (GCA) mathematics leads to the discovery of feasible solutions with quaternary GCAs, which have properties of being symmetrical, ensuring a specific count of function code words and their complements. By establishing the multivariate version of the deep hole conjecture, we find that the maximum size of the deep hole in GCAs is related to the minimum distance of the code and the code's dimension. Our investigation confirms the multivariate deep hole conjecture for quaternary GCAs of specific types and dimensions. Furthermore, we identify the unique properties of feasible quaternary GCAs and find that their solutions align with the hypercubes' vector subspaces in certain dimensions. Our analysis also indicates that the known solutions in lower dimensions meet the required criteria, and higher-dimensional solutions are computationally derived.

Recent advancements in change detection using deep neural networks have shown promising results, mainly focusing on performance enhancements. Despite using significantly more data and a more complex approach than traditional methods, little investigation has been conducted into the changes in performance and data needs when applying deep networks compared to established techniques. This study examines the changes in performance and data requirements resulting from the application of deep networks in change detection by leveraging the ASIRAC dataset, an recently created dataset for detecting land cover changes. The outcomes of this research indicate that change detection using deep networks is often unstable and demanding in terms of data, yet may not significantly outperform established methods. Consequently, supervised methods remain a viable option, offering better performance at lower data needs. Additionally, the study reveals that the consistency and reliability of change detection by deep networks can be improved through the use of ensembling techniques.

Utilizing molecular dynamics simulations and nonequilibrium molecular dynamics calculations, we explored the viscosity of dense fluids with varying densities and temperatures, specifically focusing on non-associating molecular fluids. By employing the soft-sphere potential to model particle interactions, we determined the viscosity data without data transfer and analyzed it at different temperatures and densities for the dimensions z=3, 8, and 12. A first-order approximation was applied to interpolate viscosity data across a grid of temperatures and densities, leading to density-based viscosity maps. We discovered that these viscosity maps are insensitive to density scaling when expressed through the reduced density, ultimately mimicking the behavior observed in viscothermal wave experiments.

A new model of the universe called the periodic cosmology has been created by incorporating an exact inflationary cycle into the lambda-CDM model. In this model, a lambda-CDM universe with a certain scale of inflation undergoes an inflationary cycle, resulting in a universe with a finite age and a consistent density of dark matter and neutrinos. Additionally, the model precisely calculates a universe's total entropy at its current age. Although the model initially appears promising due to its mathematical simplicity, a detailed analysis has revealed that it fails basic tests designed to evaluate its validity, particularly a test that evaluates a universe's entropy over time. Consequently, the model is unlikely to successfully explain a universe's entropy levels as it undergoes an inflationary cycle.

The concept of measurement independence is often used to demonstrate quantum nonlocality, typically through the Bell theorem. However, criticisms have been raised that traditional Bell model theory does not accurately reflect actual measurement practices. In response, researchers have proposed the use of counterfactual measurements within the quantum context. This study aims to reexamine the Bell theorem, taking into account both alternative measurements and post-selection, and reinterprets key Bell theorem outcomes in light of these considerations. Specifically, it is demonstrated that quantum theory can generate nonlocal predictions even within models of measurement independence, without the need for nonlocal communication. A new framework is established to verify the Bell theorem, one that is grounded in the principle of no superluminal communication. Unlike traditional Bell model theory, this framework distinguishes between the processes of measurement and state formation, allowing for a nuanced understanding of when data is generated by observations versus already present before measurements are taken. A key outcome of this framework is the identification of certain state properties as inherently nonlocal. In contrast, other properties are shown to be localized, including those in the Clifford algebra. A new theorem is formulated, known as the general macroscopic Sutherland theorem, which posits that any macroscopic Bell-type test can be performed using a general entangled pair of macroscopic Sutherland states.

This paper addresses the critical issue of deploying neural networks on resource-constrained devices by examining the underlying technical challenges. A comprehensive analysis under a common legal framework reveals the implementation details of neural networks on devices such as smart speakers and wearable technology. The research finds that neural networks' high memory usage and processing demands lead to power outages and processing delays. Furthermore, security concerns arise from the potential for malicious code and data extraction. To mitigate these problems, the study proposes power-efficient deep learning techniques, accelerated by hardware architectures like FPGAs and GPUs that offer opportunities for exploration.

A novel expansion of the cluster expansion for the dimer model on isorial graphs replaces the classical term-based expansion, matching whole terms instead, leading to a cleaner analysis. Utilizing this approach, we generate a cluster expansion for the number of saturated clusters of size n, resulting in a cluster expansion for the saddle point energy of the O(n) loop model, given by $\sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{\sigma^{n}}{n!} \sum_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} \prod_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{|Aut(G_{i_j}|} \mathrm{Perf}(G_{i_j})^{-1} X_{i_j}^{n} \mod n.$ Here, $G_{i_j}$ refers to the graph corresponding to vertex $i_j$, $Aut(G_{i_j})$ is the group of automorphisms for this graph, and $X_{i_j}$ represents the corresponding cluster expansion coefficient. Furthermore, $\mathrm{Perf}(G_{i_j})$ represents some element related to the cluster expansion. This novel expansion leads to a deeper understanding and confirmation of the proof of the uniformization hypothesis for these dimer models, thus making it possible to identify the limiting shape of the random cluster with specific weights assigned to vertices, as defined by $X := \sum_{i \geq 0} \frac{\sigma^{i}}

In contemporary statistics and machine learning, variable selection has become a central concern. Research on continuous data has generated numerous methods for selecting variables, but a significant gap remains when it comes to variable selection in categorical data. To bridge this gap, researchers have proposed the Group Lasso algorithm, which estimates multiple regression parameters within distinct groups and encourages sparse solutions through penalized likelihood maximization. The proposed method facilitates sparse group regression through the estimation of sparse group coefficients that allow for simultaneous selection of multiple categorical variables. As a result, the Group Lasso offers a more streamlined approach to variable selection compared to individual variables. Building on the success of the Group Lasso, this research introduces a Extended Group Lasso for selecting variables in additive models, which accommodates a broader range of model structures. The EGL is applicable to various types of additive models, including generalized additive models and Gaussian process regression. To improve efficiency, the methods employ stochastic gradient descent with accelerated Newton-CG optimization techniques. Through a comprehensive simulation study and real-world data analysis, the proposed methods demonstrate their effectiveness in variable selection and emprical results demonstrate the impact of step size on their performance.

The T-Visor scheduler is a scheduling framework designed for embedded systems, which accommodates a wide variety of embedded applications with distinct real-time requirements, including instantaneous responses, "shortest job first" precedence, and various task timing constraints. This framework has been successfully integrated into the Linux kernel and enables a diverse schedule on various platforms including ARM, x86-64, and other architectures, thus enabling various scheduling modes including system-wide scheduling and process-specific scheduling. Moreover, a user-friendly Linux utility called cschedule has been introduced, through which the real-time scheduling properties can be configured via a YAML configuration file. This integration and user-friendly interface have been illustrated by two case studies, including scheduling real-time communication on ARM-based chipboards and optimizing Linux boot time on single-board computers.

A panoramic photo capture device integrates a wide-angle lens capture panel with an IMU system, utilizing image processing to transform captured images into seamless 360-degree photographs. Although there have been previous methods developed to achieve high-quality panoramic shots, the current methods still fall short in handling images captured with high-resolution high-density cameras. Image alignment via previous methods becomes computationally intensive or inaccurate for high-resolution images. To address this, new algorithms utilizing deep learning have been developed to enhance image capture, at the cost of increased capture time. To improve upon these methods, a new image capture device is proposed, capturing images in a specific temporal order with precise temporal synchronization, allowing for efficient image processing with high levels of parallelism. A new image processing algorithm, the "diag-horiz' method, is also proposed to enhance image capture, leveraging a diagonal image representation to efficiently process images in O(1) time. Combining these advances, the proposed method allows for efficient image capture, processing, and panormatic stitching on high-resolution images, outperforming existing methods in terms of image quality, processing speed, and overall efficiency.

Research on chimeras in networks of coupled oscillators indicates that a more diverse group of oscillators tends to stabilize chimeric states.  In this study, we investigate how the distribution of mean frequencies among oscillators impacts chimera stability, focusing particularly on the limits of within-group homogeneity and the effects of infrequent interactions.  Both analytical and numerical methods are utilized to examine how the character of infrequent interactions influences chimera stability, and the results demonstrate that for systems with Infrequent Interaction Graphs, the distribution of mean frequencies is the determining factor of chimera stability, whereas for systems with Infrequent Time-Delay graphs, chimeras are more likely to occur and the distribution of mean frequencies, within-group homogeneity, and character of infrequent interactions all play roles in chimera stability.

In this research, we investigate the connection between the precision of a learned controller's internal simulator and its resilience when applied to an actual system. A well-defined likelihood lower bound derived from a Bayesian analysis of the learning process indicates that certain types of noise in the dynamics model must be minimized for the simulator to accurately reflect the behavior of the physical system. By constraining the likelihood noise at its minimum, we achieve a simulator that effectively mirrors the target dynamics with high accuracy. Moreover, this approach proves efficient in demonstrating the internal state of the controller, even when the target system contains nonlinearities like piecewise constant functions. Ultimately, this robust internal state representation results in a learned controller that remains stable under real-world conditions.

The slice algebra of a quiver with respect to a subquiver is defined using a matrix or tensor algebra over a ground ring. These algebras are specific types, with the subquiver playing a key role in their construction. Given two subquivers, one is considered preponderant if its slice algebra is equivalent to another algebra, determined by a ground ring extension. Preponderant subquivers can be characterized by various conditions, with examples also discussed. These concepts build upon prior research in the field, with the article also outlining connections to other prominent findings, including Brauer pairs(1998), algebras defined by admissible sequences(2004), and bocstable algebras(2003).

Real-world systems are often affected by non-local effects that restrict accessibility. Random tensor networks provide a suitable framework to analyze the constraints imposed by non-globally accessible sites in complex systems. By examining tensor networks where interaction strengths vary randomly, it has been found that reflected spectra, particularly the reflected 2nd R'enyi spectrum, serve as an indicator for non-globally accessible sites. Divergent behavior in the reflected spectrum was discovered in models featuring non-globally accessible sites, unlike the typical R'enyi spectrum. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that the reflected spectrum can distinguish between various random tensor network models. As a result, the reflected spectrum offers a valuable tool for identifying and characterizing constraints in complex systems, specifically applicable to models of quantum spin liquids and their extensions with globally accessible sites.

Building on previous work that introduced probability of persistence (PoP) for a limited class of dynamical systems and control problems, this study expands the concept to a broader range of advanced dynamical systems and control issues.  The research explores PoP for a comprehensive set of nonlinear control-affine systems under various interconnected dynamics.  The findings demonstrate that PoP can be a highly variable measure, even for seemingly low-dimensional systems, and can be influenced by small changes in system parameters by extremely large factors.  The study highlights the potential of PoP as a valuable tool for system design and control through the presentation of a concrete design example.

Maps of the form $f(x,y)=(\alpha-x^2-y^2,\beta-x^3-3xy)$ defined in the plane are analyzed for various $\alpha$ and $\beta$ values. The equilibrium points of these maps are studied, with periodic orbits shown to organize parameter space through a web-like structure. Within this framework, regions corresponding to non-robust periodic orbits featuring invariant circles (both internally tangent and non- internally tangent) are identified, as well as areas related to period two orbits (both robust and non-robust) mapping points to equilibrium locations along specific curves (the $\alpha$-curve, $\beta^2\alpha^{-2}$, $\alpha^{-1}$, and $\beta^{-1}$). A period two stable non-robust area is also located near the $\alpha=-1$, $\beta=1$ line. The maps in question are found to model planetary motion in a non-robust manner. The findings of this study are compared to those made in a related research paper (Chen et al., 2021), with key differences highlighted).

The holonomy in gauge theory is well understood as an integral transform along a loop. However, when applied to gravity, it becomes a complex mathematical operation. Researchers sought to reassess this concept in gravity theory, leading to a discovery of two gravity holonomies that exhibit dissimilar behaviors. One gravity holonomy follows the gauge theory model, whereas the other defies it. Furthermore, when certain gravity holonomies are applied to curved spaces, they yield inconsistent results, contradicting earlier conclusions reached in reference \cite{Makhanov:2021jro}.

For a positive integer n, let R_n be the random variable that represents the rank of n-th largest value in an independent and identically distributed sample, and let p be a real number between 0 and 1. This paper demonstrates that the cumulative distribution functions of -ln(R_n)/ln(1-p) and -ln(R_n)/ln(p) asymptotically converge to the exponential distribution with a specific parameter as n approaches infinity. Additionally, independent methods of proof are presented along with a discussion on how these results can be utilized in statistical inference.

We've developed a novel approach to tunneling time by analyzing spin tunneling through the $S_1$ $\leftrightarrow$ $S_2$ $\leftrightarrow$ $S_1$ system in which $S_1$ and $S_2$ are two consecutive energy levels of a mesoscopic magnet. This approach utilizes the real-time correlation of spin fluctuations to determine tunneling time and postulates that ATT is unaffected by temperature. An analytical formula for ATT has been derived, which reveals that the time it takes for tunneling to occur is proportional to $(\Delta E)^{-4}$ and can be accessed via spin-flip NMR, methods to validate ATT. Notably, tunneling can occur at any level of temperature, and spin fluctuations are more pronounced at higher temperatures, making ATT measurable in magnetic systems where thermal fluctuations prevail. To validate this new model, experimental results on tunneling times have been reevaluated, and the ATT has been calculated for a representative system.

In this study, we utilize the light-front relativistic quark-diquark description to work on amplitudes related to the production of P-wave charmonia states at the LHC. The results, which explicitly include relativistic corrections in amplitudes, show a reasonable match with current data for the $J/\psi(1^{3}D_{1})$ channel. While the relativistic corrections are significant for the $Y(4260)$ amplitude as well, its predicted rate is, however, higher than observed experimentally. For the $X(3872)$ amplitude, its amplitudes are largely similar to previous findings and the predicted rates are, as expected, lower.

We investigate the theoretical performance of Ramsey interferometry using a
Bose-Einstein condensate in an optical lattice. This is achieved through the
application of a rapidly switching, high-order optical pulse, implementing a
Hadamard gate through the entanglement of adjacent atoms. Our findings indicate
that higher-order gate components yield better precision and longer
available measurement time when compared to lower-order states. As a result,
better gate efficiency can be attained by increasing the order of the gate,
although this technique is hindered by noise in the optical process and atom
interaction. Nonetheless, improvements in gate efficiency can still be gained
by enhancing the higher-order components. Additionally, for a system with two
atoms, an entirely different high-order gate mechanism is discovered, where
atoms are made to interact in a multi-body state, and its higher-order state
yielding better gate efficiency under the same optical and atom interaction.
This is in contrast to lower-order gate mechanisms, specifically the two-body
entanglement which has a much faster collapse time due to lower-order states,
yet still outperforming lower-order gate mechanisms in coherence time when not
affected by noise in optical and atom interaction.

The topological structure of eBMS charges is explored, revealing a logical framework that distinguishes "soft news" vacua with degeneracies and "Schwarzian modes" along with non-degenerate states, to form a specific type of chain boundary condition. Upon partitioning the eBMS boundary, the resulting charges can be organized into two separate groups: those involving "news" charges, consisting of monodromy and bulk boundary charges, and those consisting of "Schwarzian" charges, characterized by twists and edge boundary charges. Here, both types of charges are shown to be topologically equivalent. This study also examines how both types of charges can be combined to form a more complex system, consisting of a "tetrahedron" structure, to form a specific type of eBMS charge tetrahedron. Utilizing the concept of "news" and "Schwarzian" charges, the eBMS tetrahedron is found to be a more accurate representation of eBMS charges than previously proposed models, specifically the "punctured sphere" and "Riemann surface" based on ideas by Dubois and Gopakumar, respectively.

Ensemble techniques within the machine learning community aim to boost classification precision, achieved through the utilization of multiple model iterations. However, standard ensemble methods necessitate the training of multiple networks, significantly increasing computation costs in neural network development. This paper introduces an innovative ensemble approach, ensembling residual sums, which attains a high classification precision with only a single network training, by retaining the intermediate residual values from each layer for each training sample, and re-running the network for classification prediction. Experimental outcomes reveal that the presented method surpasses state-of-the-art ensemble techniques in accuracy and requires the least number of computations, also providing thorough theoretical justification for its success.

The theory of generalized connections is an extension of traditional connections, with its potential to create new metrics that are flat in terms of the Ricci tensor. This theoretical framework has led to the development of new scalar potentials in various string theory models, with specific examples involving a non-Ricci metric and a generalized connection resulting in a flat Ricci tensor. To better understand generalized connections, this paper begins by establishing a comprehensive framework for finding metrics and scalar potentials. Focusing on one specific shape invariant example, this study provides an analytical expression for the associated scalar potential and demonstrates that additional scalar potentials can be derived from a specific harmonic one-form, with a numerical example presented for illustration.

We establish a concept of complete mapping for polynomial functions from $\mathbb{F}_q^m$ to $\mathbb{F}_q$, where $m > 0$ and $q$ represent finite fields of dimensions $m$. A specific $m$-ary function $f$ is defined as a complete mapping if for any partition of the function space into $m$ distinct subsets, where two subsets $A, B$ contain unique function values or $f(\xi)$ is the same for all $\xi \in A$ and all $\xi \in B$ respectively, and both subsets have a count of at least $\sqrt{q}$, it holds that either the function's value is the same for all inputs in set $A$ or the function's value is the same for all inputs in set $B$.

We prove a lower bound that holds for any given complete mapping $f$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^m$ to $\mathbb{F}_q$, indicating that either the function's value is the same for all inputs in set $A$ or the function's value is the same for all inputs in set $B$. Inspection of stool samples to identify intestinal parasites is currently done by visual examination, which is considered to be error-prone. We developed an image processing pipeline to assist in the analysis by leveraging the UNET architecture for image classification and segmentation tasks. The training process involved preparing images from a public dataset and testing the results using a separate dataset. The outcome of this evaluation showed that the proposed method achieved image classification accuracy of 86%, as well as precision and recall rates of 86%, when using the entire image for classification. Furthermore, the method achieved precision and recall rates of 85% when classifying images with moderate to high quality, and recall rates of 85% when classifying narrow objects with a size to diameter ratio less than 3. By segmenting objects within images, the method achieved precision and recall rates of 85% and 82%, respectively. Compared to the entire image classification process, the method achieved a 7% improvement in precision and recall rates. The outcome of the experiments confirmed that the proposed method's performance is superior to that of the UNET architecture, which achieved a recall rate of 82% in the entire image classification process. The method showed high consistency in dealing with various types of parasites, with the exception of flatworms, which may be treated as a separate category. The proposed method could potentially be used as a diagnostic tool to assist in the analysis of stool samples by providing a systematic and accurate means of analyzing visual data.

This study employs the variational approximation lie-algebra method to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, and in the process, it uses the finite difference method to validate the method. The research finds that the method can easily be extended to solve more complex problems, such as the behavior of a system's value function at the equilibrium point, and in the case of a linear 2nd order Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, it is shown that the method can be reduced to the standard variational approximation method of Poincaré's method.

This paper introduces the Genetic Filter, a control filter that enhances robustness against disturbances in quadcopter control systems. Through model predictive control techniques, the GF's efficacy is tested in guiding a quadcopter from the hover state to the state of tracking a circular path with maximum speed, while withstanding sudden environmental changes. Our simulation results prove that the combination of model predictive control and the Genetic Filter significantly improves the quadcopter's performance compared to using the Genetic Filter alone or model predictive control without it.

The pion-nucleon sigma term plays a critical role in various nuclear phenomena and precision studies. There's growing interest in this topic from both nuclear physicists and dark matter researchers. Traditionally, the sigma term can be estimated using lattice simulations, but a more accurate calculation has been elusive due to issues with lattice perturbation theory. Recent advancements in lattice simulations and a more sophisticated treatment of quarks such as chiral perturbation theory offer promising methods for the sigma term's computation. This talk will explore the differences and similarities between these two approaches, highlighting their respective challenges and potential solutions, and possibly identifying a route to achieving a more precise sigma term value.

The CMS detector's two innermost layers were upgraded with a new silicon pixel detector, implemented in 2017 as part of the CMS upgrade. Known as the Pixel Detector Component Description Document, this paper outlines the software developments in the CMS alignment section for the Pixel detector. It specifically details the geometry simulation, representation, reconstruction, and calibration techniques used for the new detector. Although the detector's format has changed, its geometry and functionality have been maintained in line with the existing design. New detector components, such as the Pixel detector's layer 3 and 4, have been incorporated into the existing code framework.

Using the XMM-COSMOS field as our primary source, we conducted an investigation to identify the host galaxies of the 193 active galactic nuclei detected at the X-ray bandwidth of 2-10 keV. We employed a two-step approach to separate the AGN activity from its host galaxy, first applying an adaptive photometry tool and then utilizing galaxy simulation to calculate the light contribution from the AGN. This resulted in a dataset of 119 AGN with host galaxies, for which we calculated the half-light radius, probabilistic redshift estimates, and likelihood ratios. These AGN host galaxies were then observed under different filters in the COSMOS optical survey, allowing us to calculate AGN and host galaxy fluxes, as well as apply various classification techniques to determine the host galaxy's stellar mass and star formation rate. We found these quantities to correlate well with theoretical Kriek models and found that the star formation rate in the host galaxies peaked at a redshift of 1.5-2. In addition, our precision in identifying the host galaxies improved at higher redshifts, achieving an impressive 75% accuracy at a redshift of 2. However, this accuracy dropped to 45% at a redshift of 0.5 due to increased noise. Furthermore, we found AGN activity to be strongly influenced by the host galaxy's mass and redshift, while showing little dependence on the host galaxy's star formation rate. The impact of neutron-star matter's density on the solar neutrino flux has long been understood, however in this research focus is placed on how neutron-star matter's asymmetry affects a neutron star' $M_R$-$R$ relation, induced by nuclear short-range correlations which in turn cause a greater neutron skin thickness. Utilizing the perturbative approach, the dependence of the $M_R$-$R$ relation and the neutron skin thickness on the nucleon-nucleon interaction parameter is studied for certain high-density neutron star matter with the $SLy4$ equation of state assumed. It was discovered that although the density affects relations for different interactions, the density has little effect on the asymmetry-induced neutron skin thickness, except for certain interactions containing $C_{0v}^{\nu}$ components which determine the density dependence of the neutron skin thickness to be weak. However, the density does affect the asymmetry-induced thickness in a positive manner for certain interactions containing $T_{0}$ components, while the density dependence of the thickness vanishes for $C_{0v}^{\nu}$ components for neutron stars with a specific normal state, indicating on the one hand that measuring the neutron skin thickness using astrophysical methods may reveal the density dependence of this thickness, while on the other hand may establish a limit on the unknown component of the $T_{0}$ interaction, however this research found that although the density dependence of this thickness is weak, it can be detected using J

We introduce an innovative complex-valued representation of RGB images based on
an anisotropic Pythagorean Gaussian that addresses both color-related and hue-based
image features. This is achieved through a geometric transformation that utilizes the
logarithm of the Euclidean distance from the red, green, and blue color axes to a predefined
origin, resulting in a single complex-valued scaling that encapsulates the interplay of the
three color channels. Furthermore, the proposed representation remains invariant under hue
shifts and exhibits robust immunity to both additive white Gaussian noise and both color and
hue distortions at the pixel level. To corroborate the enhanced robustness of the proposed
representation, the distance between corresponding points in different images is measured
and observed to be significantly lower compared to the wavelet-based scalar, particularly in
noisy scenarios. Utilizing complex-valued scaling in image filtering allows for the preservation of
high-frequency color-related details even in the presence of noise, resulting in a significant
outperformance compared to traditional methods in both color and hue-based correlation tasks.

The geometrical scaling of gluon distribution in different reactions is observed in a specific kinematic region, saturation phenomena occurs here. We apply the Balitsky-Kovchegov equation to study the gluon distribution in different reactions at similar values of the argument $x$, considering all order perturbative calculations, and find a parameter $x$ dependence in leading order, leading to geometrical scaling. We then add a simple non-linear effect to the BGGL equation, derive a non-linear equation for kinematic region where gluon distribution is not yet saturated, and obtain a partial result for parton distribution, validating key numerical results from leading order and leading twist models. Our work provides a theoretical framework for understanding saturation phenomena in gluon distribution.

A new approach is introduced where the core-collapse supernova progenitor mass distribution is randomly sampled for each event from a predetermined mass function. This method simulates the selection of individual stars from a broader mass function due to their unique and discrete occurrence. Implementing this random sampling in a galaxy simulation reveals that, under certain conditions, using a predetermined mass function for core-collapse supernovae can overestimate galaxy metal enrichment levels by as much as three times the actual amount. Additionally, using a predicted core-collapse event rate based solely on stellar mass yields inaccurate results, whereas incorporating both stellar mass and metal transfer rate of core-collapse events produces a better correlation with observational data. Finally, incorporating this novel core-collapse event model along with other improvements results in a surprisingly strong correlation between simulated and observational data on metal enrichment levels in galaxies, exhibiting a correlation coefficient of 0.94.

The performance of a predictive model with additional synthesized features can be evaluated by assessing its stability, where stable models remain superior even after being augmented with the synthesized data. In this research, a definition of model stability is introduced using outgoing training set subsets and outgoing test set subsets. The study then presents a novel concept called synthetic stability, where a model's performance with synthesized features remains superior without utilizing context-specific optimization, a technique which allows the model to be aware of the distribution of the synthesized data. The synthetic stability is experimentally validated on several classification tasks and data distributions and is further utilized to design a synthesis technique that exploits context-specific dependencies in distribution-free settings. The results demonstrate that under certain circumstances, particularly when the synthesized data distribution differs from the original data distribution, a model-specific transformation can substantially enhance the model's performance. Furthermore, the study provides empirical validation of a distribution-free context-specific transformation method for synthesized data.

Variational quantum models, such as quantum neural networks, are being developed as a first step towards applying machine learning on quantum computers. To determine the effectiveness of these models, we need to compare their performance with that of classical models. In this study, we investigate the potential differences between quantum and classical modeling performance using various output types and sizes for small-scale quantum neural networks. To do this, we train and test quantum neural networks with different output types and sizes within a machine learning framework, such as quantum circuit libraries, and compare their performance with that of classical models. The results show that the choice of output has a significant impact on the scalability of gradient-based optimization, such as backpropagation, used in quantum machine learning. Based on these findings, we recommend using outputs with a high dimensionality but restricted amplitude for small-scale quantum neural networks. Furthermore, we suggest exploring new types of outputs, such as those utilizing angular embeddings, such as the Fourier basis, as an effective alternative.

This research focuses on identifying non-existence of certain warped product submanifolds within Sasakian manifolds. Specifically, it establishes the non-existence of pointwise semi-slant and semi-slant submanifolds under specified conditions related to the direct product with a compact manifold such as $S^n$ or $S^{2n-1}$, as well as the non-existence of semi-slant and slant submanifolds within a particular type of Sasakian manifold known as the Albers-Toeplitz type. By leveraging Einstein conditions, it shows that, in the case of a semi-slant or slant submanifold being a warped product times a line, it cannot exist. Furthermore, this research builds upon and rectifies prior errors in existing literature, including those related to references 18 and 41 in the same paper.

A forward dark matter direct detection experiment can utilize a novel approach by leveraging a detector's thin and light components to detect the scattering of coherent, elastic neutrino-nucleus interactions on nuclei within the nucleus using advanced technology. By placing CHCM experiment modules at the Advanced Proton Source at Fermilab, researchers can explore a range of neutrino energies that are thousands of times higher than typical dark matter detection thresholds. With CHCM, scientists can achieve a high level of sensitivity to WIMP-nucleon cross sections, rivaling the best current experiments, all while operating at neutrino energies of 10 GeV. By combining improved detection parameters with already accomplished technology, such as Gram detector technology, it becomes possible to reach an impressive level of sensitivity to WIMPs, reaching levels over three orders of magnitude better than CHCM experiment modules alone. By using large numbers of CHCM experiment modules at the Advanced Proton Source at Fermilab, scientists can achieve a high level of sensitivity to WIMPs, reaching levels where they can detect interactions between neutrinos and specific isotopes at the level of a few events, providing valuable data for future reference. With large numbers of CHCM experiment modules, scientists can also achieve a high level of sensitivity to WIMPs by combining the data from the CHCM modules, reaching levels where they can detect interactions between neutrinos and nucleons at the level of a few times 10^-43 cm^2, providing valuable data for both dark matter and

Our investigation reveals that active dimers, where one end produces a force while the other undergoes balanced transport, exhibit steering similar to a wheel mechanism. This is compared to a device with a turning wheel, where rotation causes a pointer to move in an arc. To study this, we develop a general framework for motion based on a polynomial that dictates direction and speed at any given time. Using this approach, we analyze and solves the equations of motion for various self-dimers, demonstrating that their steering can be fully described using the same polynomial, which enables us to compare their properties with that of a standard wheel. Furthermore, we explore how external forces might influence active dimers, causing their motion to exhibit a specific non-linear pattern, akin to that produced by a curved track.

The investigation into magnetorotons within a $(1+2)$-dimensional non-fermion liquid, characterized by a massless Dirac model with a $\sigma$-term, reveals notable distinctions in their chirality between the $u=2/7$ and $u=2/9$ scenarios. While the former exhibits equal chirality in both the electron and hole variations, the latter displays opposite chirality for these variations, thus allowing the experimental verification of the recently proposed $u=2/7$ state through the examination of magnetorotons in graphene, Super-Lamb shift in muonic hydrogen, and quarkonium states, with further predictions made for observed Landau levels in graphene and hydrogenic impurities in LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interfaces.

Our investigation expands upon previous research, specifically applying our findings in the study of epidemics spreading on vast, intricate networks with numerous elements. By generalizing the results, we significantly reduce the requirements necessary to analyze the dynamics of these networks, making it easier to generate examples where the standard assumptions typically made regarding them are invalid. Unlike in [Graovac et al. (2022)], we don't limit our analysis to networks composed of networks with a specific balance, and instead, we focus on a broader range of networks, where the connection between network elements is not restricted. Furthermore, we introduce a new method to approximate and analyze more complex networks, and demonstrate that approximating and identifying subsets of networks with a specific balance is essential in understanding and predicting the evolution of epidemics on these networks. Similar to [Graovac et al. (2022)], we utilize graph partitioning and equitable partitions to analyze and understand network behavior, but now we consider all possible relaxations of these partitions and reveal how they can be used in this context. Our investigation expands on the ideas presented in [Graovac et al. (2022)] and provides new insights, examples, and methods to analyze and understand the behavior of epidemics on a broad range of networks. Just like in [Graovac et al. (2022)], we conclude that approximating and identifying relaxations of equitable partitions is crucial in understanding and predicting the behavior of epidemics on these networks.

A strong point source in a CMB map significantly affects error patterns when using biased estimators, leading to a need for map-specific corrections to biased estimators. To mitigate these discrepancies, a method utilizing a simulated SED template-derived estimator has been developed to alleviate noise in CMB maps, particularly in the channel with the strongest point source influence. By combining data from the MAMBO II survey and the LDC survey, a study created a library of point sources with diverse SEDs to simulate and recreate the map of a set of sources through a multi-channel reconstruction. By comparing reconstructed sources with actual data, a method was developed to align the simulated map with data from one channel and convert it to another, resulting in a correction applied to the 870$\mu$m map of Planck using an estimator for different frequencies, leading to negligible Planck measurement errors in reconstructed flux values. To further improve CMB map quality, a CMB model was created to estimate and subtract a diffuse background signal, followed by a re-mapping using a maximum likelihood estimator to produce an improved 870$\mu$m map with reduced noise from diffuse backgrounds, featuring an outlying source with significantly lower noise levels, reduced noise and a higher signal-to-noise ratio, particularly in CMB map quality, with a CMB model-based algorithm significantly reducing noise levels from diffuse backgrounds, resulting in a $2.23\pm 0.14$ mJy beam$^{-1}$ noise level in an improved

This paper approaches the task instruction problem using pedagogical and pragmatist theories of learning, aiming to provide more effective and efficient instruction by framing the objective as a supervised learning challenge. The task involves predicting a goal state (the target) based on initial and final states, where the key lies in identifying the crucial intervening steps rather than the entire trajectory. Drawing from theories such as implicit motor learning and John Dewey's pragmatism, it is suggested that task instruction should facilitate self-discovery, prioritizing the identification of crucial steps over full trajectories. To achieve this, a new supervised learning problem is formulated where the training data comprises initial and final states, along with diverse intermediate states, thereby encouraging the model to focus on essential steps rather than exhaustive trajectories. This approach is known as the'state-to-state' problem, where the goal is to achieve the target state by correlating the initial state with all possible goal states, thereby enabling the model to explore multiple paths to the target. It has been observed that this problem captures the essence of self-implemented learning and offers a more challenging yet efficient task instruction framework. To validate the efficacy of this approach, a new dataset has been created for a complex manipulation task, demonstrating that this method enables faster learning on a robotic platform, where the model is trained only with the initial and final states and no intermediate states. Furthermore, it has been observed that this approach can be viewed as a form of sparse reward optimization, where the key lies in engineering training

It's challenging to perform shadow tomography, a variant of quantum state tomography that uses fewer measurements than the traditional method, due to the need to post-select data from measurements made in a basis different from the basis in which the state is observed. Our research shows that when a state is followed by a projective measurement, the shadows of any state can be approximated using a specific, upper limit on the number of measurements. However, this limit depends on the specific form of the state and can be quite complex, making analytical solutions difficult to obtain. Instead, we found that when a state is followed by an ensemble of projective measurements, the shadows of any state can be approximated using a simpler, universal upper limit, independent of the state's form. This limit depends only on the number and dimensions of the measurements in the ensemble. Furthermore, we derived a formula for calculating this limit and established a condition for when the shadows of any state can be approximated using a specific, ensemble-based structure. Our research also includes a demonstration of the application of this structure, enabling shadow tomography to be performed precisely with an universal, constant limit on the number of measurements, for certain types of states.

For any convex polygons with n sides, a relationship is established that relates inradius and circumradius to n. Additionally, a relationship is found between the inradius, circumradius, and area for convex shapes in the plane. Specific relationships for unique geometric features, such as minimum perimeter and area, are also identified for specific types of convex polygons.

This study explores a challenging path-planning issue in UAV deployment, specifically focusing on speeding up user service delivery through efficient route optimization. The problem is likened to the orienteering problem, where a UAV must collect items of varying value at key locations to maximize overall gain. Theoretical research has demonstrated limited results for large-scale problems with numerous UAVs and users. To address this gap, this study proposes a cutting-plane algorithm based on a cutting plane method incorporated with a column generation approach using linear programming relaxation to enhance solution quality. The proposed algorithm is thoroughly evaluated in a simulated environment with a vast set of test cases across different scenarios.

Research on the quantum phases of bilayer graphene has revealed the unique properties of its nematic and quantum spin Hall states. Unlike single-layer graphene which exhibits symmetry under 120-degree lattice rotation, bilayer graphene exhibits symmetry under either 120-degree or 120-degree with a 180-degree supplementary rotation. Upon reaching the nematic state, the supplementary rotation symmetry disappears, while the 120-degree rotation symmetry remains intact, allowing for the formation of six-fold quasicrystalline patterns. Additionally, research has demonstrated that nematicity in bilayer graphene can be both achieved and quantified through the application of electrical bias. Notably, the electrical bias can reach a value of approximately one Kelvin. Furthermore, the control over nematicity through electrical means surpasses that of HgTe quantum spin Hall insulators in terms of versatility and reliability.

When endofullerenes adsorb on a substrate, the resulting endofullerenes exhibit diverse electronic and magnetic behaviors due to interactions between the adsorbed species, the substrate, and the enclosed atom. A computational investigation of Na@C60 on the Au(111) surface reveals the sodium atom's movement within the adsorbed fullerenes and formation of molecularly assembled structures. A computational model of the clean surface allows for the analysis of various calculations, while a simple electron charge transfer model explains the observed physisorption of Na@C60 on Au(111). Additionally, the findings of a density functional simulation match those from Scanning Tunneling Microscopy and Spectroscopy, and reveal a significant internal charge of approximately 0.85 electrons within the adsorbed Na@C60 on Au(111).

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to an surge in data generation through various devices such as sensors, cameras, and microphones, which has resulted in a high risk of security breaches and personal data exposure. To address this issue, a new paradigm called Context-Aware Internet of Things is being developed to enable context recognition and data protection in IoT systems, although this generates additional complexities for stakeholders. Therefore, an approach to safeguarding data privacy in CA-IoT ecosystems is gaining attention among researchers. This research provides an overview of the current state of data privacy concerns and proposed solutions in IoT systems, with a focus on CA-IoT. It also presents an innovative k-anonymity based technique to maintain individual anonymity during online interactions within CA-IoT.

The proposed approach consists of two stages. Firstly, data is anonymized through a k-anonymity based approach that removes identifying attributes from each data record while ensuring a certain level of anonymity. During this process, data records within a sensitive data set are grouped based on a common set of attributes called k-buckets. To ensure data anonymization, synthetic data with anonymous attributes such as location, temperature, and humidity is generated and combined with the k-buckets. Secondly, to preserve anonymized data from being de-anonymized through any inference attack, a Bayesian belief network is used to count the probability of each data record being included in a k-buckets.

In high-precision experiments, efficient data analysis and equipment operation go hand-in-hand. We introduce a novel experimental design method based on Bayesian optimization that outperforms traditional, adaptive, and random approaches in conducting low-accuracy Ramsey measurements. The proposed technique utilizes a basic model and a specific optimization strategy to drive the experiment, which we compared to two alternative protocols, demonstrating its advantages in the context of a simulated quartz crystal resonator trapped in a magnetic field. The presented method is versatile and can be applied to various situations requiring model-based optimization.

This paper explores the application of Gromov centrality in distinguishing nodes within various network configurations. It extends the original centrality, which identifies unique nodes in binary networks using irreducible Markov matrices, to multi-component networks. The Gromov centrality is calculated for a range of network types, including sparse random networks, Barabasi-Albert networks, and trees. Our findings demonstrate that this method can distinguish nodes of varying types in these networks more effectively than alternative approaches, such as eigenvector and degree centrality.

In the late 19th century, Charles Lane-Ponterrac derived a precession formula, 
which he observed to be at odds with the time-variant mean Earth-Sun distance as 
inferred from astronomical observations. This discrepancy led him to propose a 
more fundamental theory, which posits that the mean Earth-Sun distance as a 
function of time adheres to the laws of thermodynamics. The theory suggests that 
the mean Earth-Sun distance increases over time, driven by the minimization of 
the system's combined entropy, and that this process is at equilibrium due to 
the balance between entropy variation and residual dissipative forces. The theory 
was found to account for Lane-Ponterrac's observational findings and offered a 
novel explanation for the observed mean Earth-Sun distance increasing over 
time.

We demonstrate that the bundle of matrix polynomials, when considered in its full spectral context, does not form an open subset. Nevertheless, by specifying matrix polynomial families that adhere to particular spectral conditions, we establish the existence of corresponding factorizations. Consequently, these factorizations enable extraction and analysis of spectral characteristics. A key outcome of our analysis is the open nature of certain subsets derived from matrix polynomial families. Additionally, to facilitate linear algebra applications, we develop a matrix decomposition approach for these polynomial bundles, along with a corresponding algorithmic framework. A notable outcome of this approach involves a subset, denoted $S_{\lambda, \mu}$, that is open even in its closure; this subset specifically refers to matrix polynomials with specified spectral properties and rank characteristics. Furthermore, to address computational challenges associated with matrix polynomials, we develop an iterative algorithm for matrix decomposition that leverages a matrix moving-curve framework. This novel approach allows for computation on a family of matrices defined by a parameter $t$ and applies to various matrix polynomial decomposition problems. Notably, under certain conditions, the algorithm enables computation of a specific matrix decomposition for any value of $t$. Although it may not be possible to compute a decomposition for all values in a continuous and seamless manner, we can compute decompositions for a finite set of values.

Recent findings suggest that the construction of non-geometric classifying algebras in string theory can be formalized using a specific mathematical approach that utilizes continuous-trace algebras. This notion encompasses both continuous-trace and C*-algebras, offering a unifying framework that allows for an organized study of the subject. By adopting this approach, researchers can create a structured methodology for deriving and classifying non-geometric classifying algebras, which in turn can provide crucial insights into the existence of classical T-duals within non-geometric string theory. This algebraic framework has been successfully applied in recent studies to explore the existence of T-duals in several specific contexts, including torus backgrounds with flux and manifestly SL(2, R) invariance. A key outcome of this analysis was the identification of distinct non-geometric algebras that could potentially arise from torus reductions, including those describing quarter and nine-string backgrounds, as well as a specific background alleged to describe a semi-toral fold. We found that the former two correspond to the well-established general definitions of these backgrounds, but the alleged description of a semi-toral fold is actually inconsistent. Furthermore, additional geometric interpretations of the algebra can also be identified.
